Feeder Favorites.fact: Keep feeders clean by washing them every couple of weeks to protect visiting birds.

Backyard Finches.fact: Finches love nyjer and sunflower seed offered in a tube feeder.

Woodpeckers.fact: Woodpeckers drum on trees to claim territory and to find insects beneath the bark.

Owls of the Night.fact: Owls swallow small prey whole and later cough up pellets of fur and bone.

Hummingbird Garden.fact: Hummingbirds can hover and even fly backward, beating their wings dozens of times a second.

Songbirds.fact: Many songbirds sing most loudly at dawn, a time called the dawn chorus.

Birds of Prey.fact: Hawks have sharp eyesight and can spot small prey from high above the field.

Ducks and Geese.fact: Only the female mallard makes the classic quack sound.

Shorebirds.fact: Shorebirds probe the mud and sand at low tide to find small tasty creatures.

Wading Birds.fact: Herons stand very still in shallow water and then strike quickly at fish.

Sea Birds.fact: Albatrosses can glide for hours over the ocean with hardly a wingbeat.

Bird Anatomy.fact: A bird's feathers are lightweight, strong and kept tidy by daily preening.

Nests and Nesting.fact: Many birds weave spider silk into the nest to hold the twigs together.

Bird Songs and Calls.fact: Learning a few bird songs makes every walk in the garden more fun.

Seeds and Feed.fact: Black oil sunflower seed is a favorite of many backyard birds.

Feeder Types.fact: A baffle on the pole helps keep squirrels away from the feeder.

Birdbath Time.fact: Birds prefer shallow water, so add a few stones to a birdbath.

Winter Birds.fact: Birds fluff their feathers in cold weather to trap warm air close to the body.

Spring Arrivals.fact: Robins are often among the first birds to be seen on the lawn in early spring.

Summer Visitors.fact: Early morning is the best time to watch summer birds at the feeder.

Autumn Migration.fact: Many birds migrate at night using the stars and the earth's magnetic field to guide them.

Blue Birds.fact: The blue of a bluebird comes from the structure of its feathers, not from pigment.

Red Birds.fact: Male cardinals are bright red, while females are a soft tan with red touches.

Yellow Birds.fact: Goldfinches turn bright yellow in spring and olive-brown in winter.

Black and White.fact: Chickadees are curious little birds and can often be coaxed to eat from your hand.

Brown Birds.fact: Brown feathers help many birds blend into bushes and branches.

Crow Family.fact: Crows and jays are among the most clever of all birds.

Little Birds.fact: Tiny birds eat many times a day to keep their small bodies warm.

Big Birds.fact: A bald eagle's nest can be as big as a small car and is reused for years.

Flightless Birds.fact: Ostriches cannot fly, but they can run faster than most horses.

Bird Watching Gear.fact: A good pair of binoculars and a notebook are all a new birder really needs.

Bird Watching Words.fact: A lifer is the first time you ever see a certain kind of bird.

Garden Plants for Birds.fact: Plants that produce seeds and berries bring birds to the garden all year.

Trees Birds Love.fact: Old trees with holes make perfect homes for woodpeckers and owls.

Birdhouses.fact: Clean out a birdhouse each autumn so it is ready for new tenants in spring.

Eggs and Chicks.fact: Baby birds open their beaks wide and chirp loudly when a parent returns with food.

Bird Behavior.fact: Birds preen to spread natural oils over their feathers and keep them waterproof.

Bird Flight.fact: Large birds often soar on rising warm air called thermals to save energy.

Flocks and Names.fact: A group of owls is called a parliament and a group of crows a murder.

Bird Colors.fact: Birds can see colors that humans cannot, including some ultraviolet light.

Bird Foods.fact: Many seed-eating birds feed insects to their chicks because they need extra protein.

Ground Feeders.fact: Scatter seed on the ground or a low tray for birds that like to feed down low.

Thrush Family.fact: The wood thrush has one of the most beautiful flute-like songs in the forest.

Wrens and Creepers.fact: A tiny wren can be heard singing loudly from a bush or a flowerpot.

Chickadees and Titmice.fact: Chickadees hide seeds in many places and remember where they put them.

Nuthatches.fact: Nuthatches are one of the few birds that walk headfirst down a tree trunk.

Doves and Pigeons.fact: The soft cooing of a mourning dove is a familiar sound at dawn and dusk.

Kingfishers.fact: The belted kingfisher digs a nesting burrow in a riverbank.

Swallows and Swifts.fact: Swallows catch flying insects while soaring and swooping over open fields.

Flycatchers.fact: A phoebe often wags its tail while sitting on a perch.

Warbler Colors.fact: Warblers are tiny colorful birds that pass through gardens during spring migration.

Sparrows.fact: The song sparrow has many different songs and sings from a low perch.

Blackbird Family.fact: Red-winged blackbirds sing from the tops of cattails in spring.

Orioles and Tanagers.fact: Orioles are drawn to orange halves and grape jelly set out in spring.

Grosbeaks.fact: A grosbeak has a thick beak that easily cracks open large seeds.

Blue Jays and Friends.fact: Blue jays can copy the call of a hawk and may do so near feeders.

Raptors in the Sky.fact: The red-tailed hawk is often seen perched on poles along roadsides.

Peregrine Falcon.fact: The peregrine falcon is the fastest bird in a dive.

Bald Eagle.fact: Bald eagles often mate for life and return to the same nest each year.

Owl Calls.fact: The great horned owl's deep hoot can be heard on a quiet night.

Night Birds.fact: A whippoorwill repeats its name over and over on summer evenings.

Pond and Lake Birds.fact: Loons are expert divers and can stay under water for several minutes.

Marsh Birds.fact: Marsh birds hide among tall reeds and are often heard rather than seen.

Island Birds.fact: Puffins can hold several small fish in their colorful beaks at one time.

Beaks and Bills.fact: The shape of a beak tells you what a bird likes to eat.

Feathers.fact: Birds replace their old worn feathers once or twice a year in a process called molting.

Bird Feet.fact: Woodpeckers have two toes pointing forward and two backward to grip tree trunks.

Birds and Weather.fact: Birds often visit the feeder more before a storm and need extra food during snow.

Dawn Chorus.fact: Listen early in the morning, when songbirds are at their most musical.

Bird Poems and Art.fact: John James Audubon painted beautiful portraits of North American birds.

Famous Bird Lovers.fact: Roger Tory Peterson wrote one of the most famous field guides to birds.

Birds of the Farm.fact: Hens lay eggs most often in the morning and prefer a quiet, cozy nesting box.

Birds in Fairy Tales.fact: In many old stories the dove is a symbol of peace and the owl of wisdom.

Bird Sayings.fact: The early bird catches the worm, as the old saying goes.

Garden Helpers.fact: Many garden birds eat caterpillars and beetles that nibble on plants.

Insect Eaters.fact: A single pair of chickadees can feed hundreds of caterpillars to their nestlings.

Berry Lovers.fact: Cedar waxwings travel in flocks and strip berry bushes in a few days.

Birds of Latin America.fact: The resplendent quetzal has very long tail feathers in the cloud forest.

Tropical Birds.fact: Parrots are smart birds and some can learn to speak many words.

Birds of Africa.fact: Weaver birds build amazing hanging nests from woven grass.

Birds of Australia.fact: The kookaburra's loud laugh-like call rings out at dawn and dusk.

Birds of Asia.fact: Mandarin ducks are known for their dazzling colors and graceful looks.

Birds of the Arctic.fact: The ptarmigan turns white in winter to hide in the snow.

Birds of the Desert.fact: The roadrunner can race across the desert at a rapid pace.

Birds of the Woods.fact: Forest birds often sing from high in the trees where they are hard to see.

Birds of the Meadow.fact: Meadowlarks sing from fence posts across the open fields.

Birds of the Prairie.fact: Prairie chickens gather in spring and perform dancing displays.

Bird Counts and Science.fact: Counting the birds in your yard each winter helps scientists track bird populations.

Helping Birds.fact: Placing decals on windows helps prevent birds from flying into the glass.

Bird Safety.fact: Keeping cats indoors protects many songbirds, especially in nesting season.

A Day in the Birdyard.fact: Birds are usually most active at the feeder in the early morning and late afternoon.

Seasons for Birds.fact: Every season brings a different set of birds to your garden.

Pet Birds.fact: A budgie can learn to mimic words and enjoys the company of its owner.

Bird Habitats.fact: A garden with a mix of trees, shrubs and flowers can host many kinds of birds.

Birding Picnic.fact: A thermos of tea and a comfortable chair make bird watching even better.

Birds Around the House.fact: Robins and phoebes sometimes build nests on porch beams and ledges.

Birds and Flowers.fact: Tubular red flowers such as bee balm attract hummingbirds to your garden.

Bird Names with Colors.fact: Many bird names describe a color or a mark you can see in the field.

Birds Named for Sounds.fact: The chickadee and the bobwhite are named for the sounds that they make.

Friendly Backyard Birds.fact: The more kinds of food and water you offer, the more kinds of birds will visit.
